description: I've worked on AI projects involving wildfire prediction and satellite data, and I'm interested in using technology to solve real-world problems. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I want to work with a team that enjoys building creative solutions and learning new skills.
summary: AgriLens is a free web app that turns NASA data into simple, practical advice for farmers anywhere on Earth. A farmer clicks their field on a map and picks one of 53 crops. AgriLens then downloads 35 years of daily NASA POWER data for that exact spot. It gives four answers. The Season Outlook shows the odds of a dry spell, crop-damaging heat or too much rain over the next 30, 60 or 90 days. It finds the past years whose soil moisture and rain looked most like today, and checks what happened next. The Pest & Disease Risk tab uses published weather rules for diseases like rusts, blights and rice blast, plus insect growth speed, to tell farmers when to check their fields. Best Crops Here scores every crop on how well the local climate suits it, and says which crop types are not recommended and why. A farm to-do list, a Simple mode and “Explain simply” buttons keep it easy for farmers without technical training. AgriLens also tests itself on past seasons and shows its accuracy score, so farmers know how much to trust it.
details:
What it does: AgriLens helps farmers adapt to changing weather by turning NASA Earth data into plain-language decisions: what to plant, when to save water, and when to scout for pests.

How it works:

  1. Season Outlook (“analog forecast”). It measures the farm’s current root-zone soil wetness, rain over the last 30 and 90 days, and temperature. It finds the 7 most similar past years on the same calendar date since 1991 and counts how many had a dry, very wet or heat-stress next 30/60/90 days. It compares that with the normal odds to set the risk level. It tests itself by forecasting each past year using only the other years, and shows a Brier skill score.
  2. Pest & Disease Risk. It applies simplified temperature, humidity and rain rules for each crop family to the last 14 days of NASA data. Insect growth speed uses growing degree days compared with normal.
  3. Best Crops Here. It compares 35 years of monthly NASA temperature and rain against the climate needs of 53 major world crops, simplified from FAO crop data. It gives each crop a 0–100 fit score, the best planting window, and whether irrigation is needed. It lists the crop types that are not recommended, with reasons such as “winters too cold”.
  4. Farmer-friendly design: a farm to-do list, Simple mode that hides technical detail, “Explain simply” buttons, crop search, “Use my location”, and a full-screen map.

Benefits and impact: it works for any farm on Earth, including smallholders with no weather station. Advice comes as clear actions, not raw charts. It is honest about uncertainty: it shows odds, the past years used, and its own test score.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page with no server, calling the NASA POWER API directly from the browser. Leaflet for the map, with Esri / CARTO / OpenStreetMap map tiles.

Creativity: it combines a long-range analog forecast, pest alerts and crop suitability in one simple app. It also checks its own accuracy and tells farmers when not to trust the forecast.

What we considered: farmers with low technical literacy, worldwide coverage, data delays (it shows the last available date), and the limits of 50 km data resolution.
